usage: 소 + 가 because 소 ends in a vowel
all animals are counted with 마리, never 개
키우다 = to raise/keep an animal, takes 를
examples: Counter 마리 sits after the number, before 를.
Animal cries use 울다; 음매 is the Korean 'moo'.
nuance: 소 is the live animal — a cow or ox grazing in a field. The crucial trap for English speakers is that the meat is a completely different word: 소고기 (소 'cow' + 고기 'meat'), so ordering '소' at a restaurant sounds like you want a whole live animal. Compare 소 with the loanword 우유 territory — milk is 우유 (牛乳, 'cow-milk'), not 소 something. 소 is one syllable ending in a vowel, so it always takes the subject marker 가 (소가), and like every animal it is counted with 마리, never 개 (which is for inanimate objects). A second pitfall: the verb for the cow's sound is 울다 'to cry', the same verb used for nearly all animal noises, so 소가 울어요 is natural even though English would never say a cow 'cries'.

Counting cows with 개 (소 한 개). 개 is for objects; animals always take 마리, so say 소 한 마리.
Using 만들다 'make' for raising a cow. To keep/raise a live animal the verb is 키우다, so 소를 키워요.

usage: 쥐 + 가 because 쥐 ends in a vowel
examples: There's a mouse in the kitchen!
Existence at a place: 부엌에 + 쥐가.
Past tense 잡다 → 잡았어요; 쥐 is the object.
쥐 한 마리가 벽 뒤로 숨었어요.
A mouse hid behind the wall.
숨다 = to hide; 마리 counts the one animal.
nuance: 쥐 covers both 'mouse' and 'rat' — Korean does not lexically split the small one from the big one the way English does, so context (or 큰 쥐 'big rat') carries the difference. The number-one pitfall is the computer device: a computer mouse is the loanword 마우스, never 쥐, so 쥐 클릭 would baffle a listener. Culturally 쥐 carries a negative, dirty, sneaky image (it is also the first animal of the zodiac, 쥐띠 'born in the year of the Rat'). It is one syllable ending in a vowel, so it takes 가 (쥐가), and as an animal it is counted with 마리. Note the verb pairing: you 잡다 'catch/trap' a 쥐, and a cat 잡다 it too — the same verb works for the hunter and the trap.

usage: 뱀 + 이 because 뱀 ends in the consonant ㅁ
뱀 + 을 because it ends in a consonant
examples: Plain-form exclamation 이다 → 이다! after a consonant.
I saw a snake on the mountain.
Object 뱀을; 한 마리 can float before the verb.
The snake slithered through the grass.
지나가다 = pass through; 스르르 mimics slithering.
nuance: 뱀 is a snake, and for learners it is a perfect drill word for the consonant-ending particle rule: because 뱀 ends in ㅁ, the subject marker is 이 (뱀이, never 뱀가) and the object marker is 을 (뱀을, never 뱀를). This single word trips up beginners who default to 가/를 after every noun. There is no Sino-Korean layer here — 뱀 is pure native Korean. It is counted with 마리 like all animals. Watch the adjective 무섭다 'scary': it is ㅂ-irregular, so 'snakes are scary' becomes 뱀이 무서워요 (the ㅂ turns into 워), not 무섭어요. Snakes carry an ominous, sometimes sly cultural image, and 뱀 also names the zodiac sign 뱀띠 'year of the Snake'.

Conjugating 무섭다 as 무섭어요. It is ㅂ-irregular: 무섭다 → 무서워요, so 뱀이 무서워요.

usage: 개구리 + 가 because it ends in a vowel
animal sounds use 울다, not 노래하다
examples: 폴짝 is the mimetic word for a light hop.
There are two frogs in the rice paddy.
논 = rice paddy; 마리 counts them.
When it rains the frogs go 'ribbit'.
개굴개굴 is the Korean frog sound + 울다.
nuance: 개구리 is a frog, a four-syllable native word that learners must keep whole — dropping the final 리 to say 개구 is a common slip. The big pitfall is the verb for its sound: Korean uses 울다 'to cry' for almost every animal noise, so a frog 'croaks' as 개구리가 울어요, never 노래하다 'sing' and never 말하다. The onomatopoeia is 개굴개굴 (the English 'ribbit'). Distinguish the life stages: a tadpole is a separate word, 올챙이, and there is even a proverb 개구리 올챙이 적 생각 못 한다 ('the frog forgets its tadpole days', i.e. people forget their humble beginnings). It ends in a vowel so it takes 가 (개구리가), and it is counted with 마리.

usage: 벌레 + 가 because it ends in a vowel
examples: There's a bug in the room.
Existence at a place: 방에 + 벌레가.
I caught the bug with a tissue and threw it out.
작은 벌레 한 마리가 스멀스멀 기어가요.
A tiny bug is creeping along.
nuance: 벌레 is the everyday, slightly negative catch-all for a creepy-crawly — a bug, insect, or worm you would rather not see. The sharp contrast learners need is 벌레 vs 곤충: 곤충 (昆蟲, the Sino-Korean term for 'insect') is the neutral, scientific six-legged classification you meet in textbooks and museums, while 벌레 is the casual spoken word loaded with a faint 'yuck'. So a child at a science class says 곤충, but the same child screaming in the bathroom says 벌레. 벌레 also extends figuratively to a person obsessed with something (공부벌레 'study-bug', i.e. a bookworm). It ends in a vowel, taking 가 (벌레가), and even the tiniest creature is counted with 마리, never 개.

usage: 모기 + 가 because it ends in a vowel
I got bitten by a mosquito
active 물다 = to bite; 모기 + 가
examples: There are lots of mosquitoes in summer.
Topic 여름에는 sets the season; 모기가 많다.
I got a mosquito bite so it's really itchy.
밤새 모기 한 마리가 윙윙거려서 못 잤어요.
One mosquito buzzed all night so I couldn't sleep.
윙윙거리다 = to buzz; 마리 counts it.
nuance: 모기 is a mosquito, and the must-learn point is the bite construction. English says 'a mosquito bit me' (mosquito = subject), but the natural Korean is the passive: 모기에 물렸어요 'I was bitten by a mosquito', where 물리다 is the passive of 물다 'to bite' and the biter is marked with 에, not 가. Saying 모기가 물렸어요 wrongly makes the mosquito the one bitten. If you want the mosquito as the actor you must use active 물다: 모기가 나를 물었어요. The itch that follows is 가렵다 'itchy' (an adjective), and the buzzing is 윙윙. 모기 ends in a vowel, taking 가, and is counted with 마리. It is a constant Korean summer complaint, so this passive bite phrase is extremely high-frequency.

Counting mosquitoes with 개. They take 마리: 모기 한 마리.

usage: 나비 + 가 because it ends in a vowel
the butterfly perched on the flower
examples: 꽃에 나비 한 마리가 살포시 앉았어요.
A butterfly gently landed on the flower.
Now that it's spring, there are more butterflies in the garden.
nuance: 나비 is a butterfly — a pretty, positive native word, unlike most bug vocabulary. Two distinctions matter. First, a moth is 나방, a different (and far less charming) creature, so do not let the similar shapes 나비/나방 blur. Second, the verb for landing on a flower is 앉다 'to sit/perch', the same verb as sitting on a chair, so 꽃에 나비가 앉았어요 is the natural image, not 서다 'stand'. The flying verb 날다 is ㄹ-irregular, so 'it flies' is 날아요. 나비 ends in a vowel, taking 가, and is counted with 마리. The onomatopoeia for its flight is 훨훨. 나비 is also a beloved cat name in Korea, roughly the equivalent of 'Whiskers' or 'Kitty'.

usage: 거미 + 가 because it ends in a vowel
거미줄 = web; the set verb is 치다, not 만들다
examples: There's a spider on the ceiling.
The spider spun a web in the corner.
거미줄 + 치다 is the natural pairing.
nuance: 거미 is a spider, a native word ending in a vowel, so it takes 가 (거미가). The key collocation to learn as a chunk is the web: 거미줄 is a compound of 거미 'spider' + 줄 'line/thread', and the idiomatic verb for spinning one is 거미줄을 치다 'to set/string a web', not 만들다 'make' — using 치다 (the same verb as in 줄을 치다 'string a rope') marks you as natural. Note that, strictly, a spider is an arachnid, not a 곤충 'insect', but in everyday speech Koreans lump it in with 벌레 'bugs' anyway. It is counted with 마리. The adjective 무섭다 'scary' is ㅂ-irregular, so 거미가 무서워요, not 무섭어요.

Counting spiders with 개. They take 마리: 거미 한 마리.

usage: 땅 + 이 because it ends in the consonant ㅇ
땅 + 에 marks the location of resting
examples: The child sat on the ground.
The land here is really wide.
I dug the ground and planted a small tree.
nuance: 땅 is the native word for the ground, land, or soil under our feet, and it stretches from the physical dirt you 파다 'dig' to the legal land you 사다 'buy'. The biggest English-speaker trap is 'Earth': the planet is 지구 (地球, 'earth-sphere'), never 땅, so '지구가 둥글다' (the Earth is round), not 땅. Distinguish three near-neighbors: 땅 = ground/land in general; 흙 = the soil/dirt as a substance you hold in your hand; 토지 (土地) = land as a formal real-estate/legal term. 땅 ends in the consonant ㅇ, so it takes 이 (땅이, never 땅가) and the object 을 (땅을). To sit or fall 'on' the ground, mark the spot with 에: 땅에 앉다.

Saying 땅가 넓어요. After the final consonant ㅇ you must use 이: 땅이 넓어요.

usage: for a fire to break out
set phrase; 불 + 이 + 나다, never 불이 시작하다
to put out a fire / turn off a light
to light a fire / turn on a light
examples: 끄다 → 꺼; 좀 softens the request.
The room is dark. I'll turn on the light.
A fire broke out in the neighbor's kitchen.
불이 나다 → 났어요, the fixed 'fire starts' phrase.
nuance: 불 is a single native word covering two ideas English keeps apart: 'fire' (flames) and the 'light' of a lamp. So 불을 켜다 / 불을 끄다 means both 'light/extinguish a fire' and 'switch a light on/off' — context decides. The verb pair to memorize is 켜다 (on) / 끄다 (off); never use 열다 'open' / 닫다 'close' for lights, the way some learners do by analogy with English 'open the light'. For a fire breaking out, the fixed phrase is 불이 나다 'a fire occurs' (with 나다 'to come out'), not 불이 시작하다. 불 ends in ㄹ, so it takes 이 (불이, never 불가). Watch the irregulars: 끄다 is ㅡ-irregular (끄다 → 꺼요) and 뜨겁다 'hot' is ㅂ-irregular (뜨거워요). Related: 불꽃 = flame/spark, 모닥불 = campfire.

usage: 공기 + 가; 맑다 is the set adjective for clean air
공기 + 가; used for polluted/stuffy air
examples: The mountain air is so fresh.
I opened the window and breathed in fresh air.
요즘 미세먼지 때문에 공기가 너무 나빠요.
The air is really bad these days because of fine dust.
미세먼지 때문에 = because of fine dust.
nuance: 공기 is the air we breathe, a Sino-Korean word: 空氣 ('empty-energy/vapor'), the same 氣 'qi/energy' seen in 기분 'mood' and 날씨-adjacent 일기. Two boundaries matter. First, do not confuse 공기 'air' with 날씨 'weather' or 기후 'climate' — they are different concepts, and '오늘 공기 좋다' (good air today) is not the same as '오늘 날씨 좋다' (good weather today). Second, the natural collocation for clean air is 공기가 맑다 'the air is clear', slightly more idiomatic than 공기가 깨끗하다 'clean'; bad air is 공기가 나쁘다. Note that 공기 'to breathe' uses 마시다, literally 'to drink/inhale'. For pollution the everyday term is 미세먼지 'fine dust'. (Beware a homophone: 공기 also names a children's game of jacks and a bowl of rice — context separates them.)

Saying 공기를 숨 쉬다. To breathe air the verb is 마시다 (inhale) or just 숨을 쉬다 'to breathe'; you don't pair 공기 with 숨 쉬다 directly.
Always reaching for 깨끗하다 for clean air. The more idiomatic set phrase is 공기가 맑다 'the air is clear'.

usage: 오렌지 + 가 because it ends in a vowel
whole fruit is counted with 개, not 마리
fixed compound; 주스 is also a loanword
examples: I eat an orange in the morning.
One glass of orange juice, please.
This orange is sweet and tangy.
nuance: 오렌지 is the imported orange, written as a loanword straight from English. The essential contrast is with 귤 (gyul), the native Korean tangerine/mandarin: 귤 is the small, easy-peel, winter-staple citrus that Koreans actually eat by the boxful at home, while 오렌지 is the bigger, thicker-skinned imported fruit usually bought for juice. Calling a 귤 an 오렌지 (or vice versa) is a real giveaway. As a loanword its spelling is fixed — 오렌지, not 오린지 or 오랜지. Being inanimate fruit, it is counted with 개 (오렌지 한 개), never the animal counter 마리; a glass of its juice is counted with 잔. The taste vocabulary that pairs with it is 새콤달콤하다 'sweet and tangy' and 달다 'sweet'.

examples: I sliced chili and added it to the stew.
You need plenty of chili powder for kimchi to turn red.
nuance: 고추 is the chili pepper, the backbone of Korean spice, and it spawns a small family you should keep straight: ground it becomes 고춧가루 'chili powder' (note the 사이시옷 — an inserted ㅅ for the compound, so 고춧가루, not 고추가루); the fermented red paste is 고추장; a fresh green chili is 풋고추. The sharpest pitfall is 고추 vs 후추: 후추 is black pepper, a totally different seasoning, so swapping them ruins a recipe. The adjective for its heat is 맵다 'spicy', which is ㅂ-irregular (맵다 → 매워요), not 매웠다-style regular. Inanimate, it is counted with 개. Culturally 고추 is loaded — its red color symbolized a baby boy, and it is also slang for a little boy's genitals, so the word carries a knowing double meaning adults will recognize.

usage: to watch a movie at the cinema
극장 + 에서 marks where the action happens
극장 + 이 because it ends in the consonant ㅇ
to meet in front of the theater
examples: I go to the cinema on weekends.
I watched a movie at the theater.
Let's meet in front of the theater at 7.
극장 앞 + 에서 marks the meeting spot.
nuance: 극장 is a place to watch a show — historically a live theater, today most often a movie cinema. It is Sino-Korean: 劇場 ('drama-place', 劇 'play/drama' + 場 'place/arena', the same 場 in 시장 'market' and 운동장 'sports field'). The register/usage contrast to know is 극장 vs 영화관: 영화관 (映畵館, 'movie-hall') specifically means a film cinema and sounds a touch more modern, while 극장 is the older, broader word that still covers cinemas and is universally understood — a multiplex like CGV is fine to call either. The grammar drill here is the 에 vs 에서 split: use 에 for the destination you go to (극장에 가다) but 에서 for the location where an action occurs (극장에서 영화를 보다). Because 극장 ends in ㅇ, it takes 이 (극장이, never 극장가).

Assuming 극장 means only a live-play theater. In everyday Korean it usually means the movie cinema; the live-stage nuance is context-dependent.

usage: to buy a book at the bookstore
서점 + 에서 marks where you buy
서점 + 이 because it ends in the consonant ㅁ
examples: I bought a book at the bookstore.
권 counts books; 서점에서 = where you bought.
There's a bookstore near the school.
Want to go to the bookstore together this weekend?
nuance: 서점 is a bookstore, where you buy books. It is Sino-Korean: 書店 ('book-shop', 書 'book/writing' + 店 'store', the same 店 in 편의점 'convenience store' and 음식점 'restaurant'). The contrast every beginner must lock in is 서점 vs 도서관: a 서점 is a shop where you pay and own the book, whereas 도서관 (圖書館, 'library') is where you borrow and return — confusing them produces sentences like 'I bought a book at the library'. A nearly synonymous word is 책방, a warmer, more old-fashioned native-flavored term for a (often small) bookshop. The grammar point is the same 에/에서 contrast: 서점에 가다 (go to) but 서점에서 책을 사다 (buy at). Since 서점 ends in ㅁ, it takes 이 (서점이, never 서점가); books inside are counted with 권.

usage: to go to the hair salon
to get a haircut at the salon
미용실 + 이 because it ends in the consonant ㄹ
examples: I'm going to the hair salon tomorrow.
I got my hair cut short at the salon.
I booked the salon — I'm going to get a perm.
nuance: 미용실 is a hair/beauty salon where you cut, dye, or perm your hair. It is Sino-Korean: 美容室 ('beauty-grooming-room', 美 'beauty' + 容 'appearance/grooming' + 室 'room', the same 室 in 교실 'classroom' and 화장실 'restroom'). The contrast to know is 미용실 vs 이발소: an 이발소 (理髮所, 'barbershop') is the traditional men's barber — think the spinning pole — and now sounds old-fashioned, while 미용실 serves everyone and is the default modern word; younger speakers also say the loanword 헤어숍 or just 미용실. The key collocation is 머리를 자르다 'to cut one's hair' (literally 'cut the head'), with 자르다 → 잘랐어요 in the past. Note 머리 here means 'hair', not 'head', in this context. Since 미용실 ends in ㄹ, it takes 이 (미용실이, never 미용실가).
